answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account-level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for MongoDB-compatible accounts). Example ARM/Bicep resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example commands: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB; az cosmosdb show --name myAccount --resource-group myRg. This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb) rather than a separate extension.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Example Bicep: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." kind = "MongoDB" ... }).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string for Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB Mongo API): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<accountName>@. For SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true); port for non-SRV TLS connections is 10255.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: There are multiple provisioning models: traditional Cosmos billing by Request Units (RU/s) (provisioned throughput or autoscale), a serverless option for some workloads, and newer vCore-based dedicated compute SKUs for MongoDB-compatible clusters (vCore tiers like M-series). Depending on the account SKU you will be billed by RU/s or by vCore allocation. (Expect to choose either RU/s or a vCore compute tier when creating the account.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary data-plane auth for MongoDB-compatible accounts is username/password using the account keys (the connection string contains the username and primary/secondary key as password) and standard MongoDB SCRAM auth. Historically Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication is not supported for MongoDB wire protocol data connections; Entra ID is used for management/RBAC via ARM but not as a driver auth mechanism for the MongoDB API. Use the provided connection string/primary key for drivers.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the data plane. For Python, use pymongo (pip install pymongo). There is no special service-specific data-plane SDK for Mongo operations; Azure provides management SDKs (Azure SDK for Python) for provisioning and ARM operations but for database access use the official MongoDB driver.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector indexes on Mongo-compatible DocumentDB are typically created using MongoDB-style kNN vector indexes (e.g., knnVector) and can use algorithms like HNSW (or DiskANN/IVF on some SKUs). Example createIndex command (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.providers.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } } ) — adjust dimensions and method params for your embeddings. (This is the shape of the command you should issue.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/search functionality is done either via the MongoDB "search" (Atlas Search style) aggregation stage ($search) if the service exposes Atlas-like search indexes, or by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search for Cosmos DB accounts when you need richer hybrid queries. Hybrid vector+text ranking is typically done with a combined query stage that uses the vector index for nearest-neighbors plus text predicates/boosting (e.g., a compound $search with vector and text clauses or an application-side hybrid ranker that combines cosine scores with text match scores).

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported wire protocol/server versions depend on the account SKU; recent offerings support MongoDB 6.0 and 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Some MongoDB features historically missing or different include server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages or operators, and certain transaction/replica-set behaviors — always test your workload. Expect most common CRUD, aggregation, and driver APIs to work but verify advanced features (e.g. DB-level users, some admin commands) in your cluster.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator that replicates the Azure DocumentDB Mongo API feature set. For local development run a vanilla MongoDB Docker image (for feature parity pick the same server version the cluster advertises, e.g. mongo:7.0) and bind to the standard port 27017: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0. Use this for local integration tests, but validate against the real cluster for Azure-specific behaviors (indexes/knn algorithms).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams (watch) are supported when the cluster exposes a replica-set/oplog and the Mongo wire-protocol compatibility level includes change-stream support (newer MongoDB-compatible clusters do). Typically no additional per-collection flag is required, but the account/cluster SKU must support change streams; ensure the user has the needed privileges and test watch() on the target collection. If change streams are not supported on your SKU you will get an error.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane inspection/agent tools for Azure DocumentDB (Mongo-compatible); the general Azure MCP server does not expose the service-specific documentdb data-plane inspection tools. The prompt indicates a documentdb MCP server with profile 'default' is provided — use that.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally used the name DocumentDB for the original Cosmos DB (SQL) service; Cosmos DB superseded DocumentDB. Azure "DocumentDB" historically referred to what is now Azure Cosmos DB. The open-source "DocumentDB" projects (if any) are unrelated; Azure's DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a proprietary Microsoft service that offers multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra-compatible, Gremlin, Table).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Microsoft Azure's Cosmos DB storage/engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility (it is not a stock mongod process). In practice you use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect some behavioral differences and missing admin features; thoroughly test aggregation pipelines, transactions and any advanced server-side code. Use the MongoDB driver APIs unchanged but validate behavior against the platform.

answers.question: What database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_healthcare_20 for all sample collections and indexes (do not touch other databases).

answers.question: What vector index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a knn vector index on the providers collection embedding field. Example Mongo shell command: db.providers.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } } ) — change dimensions to match your embedding model.

answers.question: What exact connection code will the sample use at runtime to open a client?
answers.answer: Read the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient. Example Python: import os from pymongo import MongoClient client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000) db = client['sample_healthcare_20']

answers.question: Which Python library will the sample use to talk to the DB and to store vectors?
answers.answer: Use pymongo for MongoDB-compatible operations (pip install pymongo). Store vectors as a numeric array field e.g. 'embedding': [0.123, 0.456, ...] and use the createIndex command above to create the vector index. For LlamaIndex integration, generate embeddings with your embedding model and insert documents with that embedding field.

answers.question: Which authentication credential will the sample use for data-plane access?
answers.answer: Use the account primary connection string (username and primary key) placed in the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable for data-plane access; Azure AD-based driver auth is not used for this sample.
